findings.location: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 2(a), tex lines 371-373
findings.quote: a sum of per-step functions has zero mixed second difference for two observations at different steps (window theorem, project note), whereas $\log\sum_ce^{\lambda(g,c)}$ has a non-zero one under A1.
findings.problem: The class statement is about the normalized posterior q(g), whose log contains the normalizer log Z(o), which also has non-zero mixed second differences. The exclusion must therefore be argued on log-odds between goal values: sum_t [h_{g,t}-h_{g',t}] has zero mixed second difference, while the log-odds of optimal Bayes, log sum_c e^{lambda(g,c)} - log sum_c e^{lambda(g',c)}, has a non-zero one. As written, a non-zero mixed difference of log sum_c e^{lambda(g,c)} that were the same for every g would cancel and not exclude the class. The non-zero statement is also asserted, not shown.

findings.quote: multiplies the input-dependent power by $\sigma_w^2/2=\tfrac16$, which is also the slope $\chi$ of its correlation map at $c=1$: the ordered phase of signal propagation, in which all inputs converge to one point
findings.problem: The slope of the normalized correlation map at c=1 equals sigma_w^2/2 only at the length fixed point set by the bias (q* = sigma_b^2/(1-1/6), here 4e-4 at N=1000). While the input-dependent power exceeds the bias floor, the ReLU map's slope at c=1 is close to 1 (bias-free ReLU is critical in Poole's normalized map; numerator and denominator both shrink by 1/6). The measured c_k shows exactly this: 1-c_k contracts by 0.93, 0.70, 0.54, 0.28, 0.17 per layer, reaching 1/6 only from k~4, after the input-dependent power (0.0026 at k=1, 0.0004 at k=2, 0.0001 at k=3) has fallen below the floor (0.0003-0.0004). Consequently the depth scale 6 xi_c = 3.4 layers (line 244) counts from the fixed point and undercounts the first layers; the convergence 'to one point' is driven by PyTorch's non-zero bias, which the text does not mention.

findings.quote: Its canonical cost, the $\tfrac k2\log n$ of a two-part code for $k$ parameters (Rissanen 1978; Schwarz 1978), would make larger learners pay more regret. Within a family the opposite holds \st{measured}
findings.problem: The (k/2) log n term is the regret of the two-part or prequential (Bayes-mixture) code relative to the best member of the k-parameter class, per sample, for regular identifiable models. The measured cumulative regret is relative to optimal Bayes, a fixed reference outside the smaller classes, in nats x updates (batches of episodes). In a nested family the larger class's best member is closer to optimal Bayes, so regret against optimal Bayes can fall with k while regret against each class's own best member still grows like (k/2) log n. The sentence presents the measurement as the opposite of the MDL penalty, but the two quantities have different comparators; the data do not contradict MDL/BIC. Also 'k' in the penalty is the effective dimension, not the raw count, for non-identifiable networks.

'No fixed sample can be overfitted' concerns the generalization gap E[R(f~)-R_n(f~)], not E_est as defined in eq. 2 (risk of the empirical minimizer of n examples versus the best member); with streaming the empirical minimizer is never formed, so E_est and E_opt are not separately identified and 'negligible' is not elementary. Line 288 then explains the within-family regret by larger networks being 'more sample-efficient', which is a finite-sample (estimation) property, in tension with E_est negligible.
